title: Pseudo-classes and Pseudo-elements
summary: CSS can style a page part when it is in a certain state, such as a link under a mouse pointer.
introduction: CSS can style a page part when it is in a certain state, such as a link under a mouse pointer. You can also style a small part of an element. Try one state at a time, including the focus state used by a keyboard.
learningObjectives: Select elements by position with :first-child, :last-child and :nth-child()
Generate decorative content with ::before and ::after and style parts with ::marker and ::first-letter

blocks.text: A pseudo-class starts with a single colon and matches an element only while it is in a particular state. Links have four: `:link` (not yet visited), `:visited`, `:hover` (pointer over it) and `:active` (being pressed). Because these rules usually have the same specificity, their order decides which wins when several apply at once, so write them in that order: link, visited, hover, active. `:focus` matches an element that has keyboard focus or was just clicked; `:focus-visible` matches only when the browser would show a focus ring, which in practice means keyboard navigation, so it is the right hook for custom focus styles.
Run it, then hover the link and the button, and press Tab to move focus onto them: the orange ring appears for keyboard focus but not for a mouse click, which is exactly the behaviour users expect.

Structural pseudo-classes pick elements by their place among siblings. `:first-child` and `:last-child` are self-explanatory; `:nth-child()` takes a formula of the form `an+b`, where `n` counts from 0, so `2n` selects the even positions, `2n+1` the odd ones, `n+3` everything from the third onwards and `-n+3` the first three. The keywords `odd` and `even` are accepted too. These count *every* sibling regardless of type; `:nth-of-type()`, `:first-of-type` and `:last-of-type` count only siblings of the same element type.

blocks.text: Form controls expose their state to CSS: `:checked`, `:disabled` and `:enabled`, `:required`, `:valid` and `:invalid`, `:placeholder-shown`. `:invalid` is true as soon as the page loads, before the user has typed anything, so a red border on `:invalid` shouts at people prematurely; `:user-invalid` waits until they have interacted with the field, which is what a form should do. `:empty` matches elements with no children at all. And `:has()` lets you reach *outward*: style the label that contains a checked box, or the form that contains an invalid field.

blocks.title: Rendered output after the checkbox has been ticked

blocks.text: Type an incomplete address into the email field and move away from it: the red border appears only after you have interacted, thanks to `:user-invalid`. Tick the box and its label turns bold through `:has()`.

A pseudo-element starts with a double colon and styles a *part* of an element or adds a part that is not in the HTML. `::before` and `::after` insert a box as the first or last child, and that box only exists if the rule sets `content`, even an empty string. `::first-letter` and `::first-line` target the typographic parts of a block of text, `::marker` is the bullet or number of a list item, `::placeholder` the hint text in a field and `::selection` the highlighted text. Browsers still accept the old single-colon spelling `:before` for the original four pseudo-elements, but write the double colon so the difference from pseudo-classes stays visible.

blocks.title: No content, no pseudo-element
blocks.text: A `::before` or `::after` rule without a `content` declaration generates nothing, however many other properties it sets; add `content: "";` for purely decorative boxes. And never put essential text or icons-with-meaning into generated content: screen readers handle it inconsistently and users cannot select or copy it. Decoration only.

blocks.title: One colon or two?
blocks.text: Pseudo-*classes* describe a state of an existing element and use one colon (`:hover`). Pseudo-*elements* describe a part of an element and use two (`::before`). If you can ask "is the element currently…?" it is a pseudo-class; if you can ask "which piece of the element?" it is a pseudo-element.

questions.question: Which selector matches the 2nd, 4th and 6th items of a list?
questions.explanation: `:nth-child(even)` (or `2n`) selects the even positions. `:nth-child(2)` selects only the second item and `:first-child` only the first.

questions.question: `::before` and `::after` generate nothing unless the rule includes a `content` declaration.
questions.explanation: The `content` property creates the pseudo-element's box. Without it, nothing is generated, whatever else the rule sets.
